summary: 1 Kings 13 (34 verses) continues the story of wisdom to idolatry. Starting with 'Behold, a man of God came out of Judah by Yahweh’s word to Bethel; and Jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense.', it moves through themes of wisdom to idolatry, divided kingdom and calls readers toward divided kingdom.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows wisdom to idolatry lived out in solomon to exile. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Behold, a man of God came out of Judah by Yahweh’s word to Bethel; and Jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense.
He said to him, “I also am a prophet as you are; and an angel spoke to me by Yahweh’s word, saying, ‘Bring him back with you into your house, that he may eat bread and drink water.’” He lied to him.
This thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, even to cut it off and to destroy it from off the surface of the earth.

questions.question: What is happening in 1 Kings 13?
questions.answer: In 34 verses, this chapter 1 kings 13 (34 verses) continues the story of wisdom to idolatry. starting with 'behold, a man of god came out of judah by yahweh’s word to bethel; and jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense.', it moves through themes of wisdom to idolatry, divided kingdom and calls readers toward divided kingdom. The setting is solomon to exile, written to exiles. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote 1 Kings and why 13 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally prophetic history, addressed to exiles around ~550 bc compiled. This chapter fits the book's purpose as kings history — its themes of wisdom to idolatry, divided kingdom build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'prophet' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Messenger speaking for God. In this chapter, it appears in context of wisdom to idolatry. For a first-time reader: think of it as messenger speaking for god, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through wisdom to idolatry and divided kingdom, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 26 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'When the prophet who brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, “It is the man of God who was disobedient to Yahweh’s word. Therefore Yahweh has delivered him to the lion,...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about wisdom to idolatry. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
